# macOS Updates - full knowledge file

> macOS Updates is a free, open-source (MIT) one-command update orchestrator for Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 13 to 27. One run updates macOS, Mac App Store apps, Homebrew formulae and casks, native CLI tools plus npm globals, and 46 internet-downloaded apps. It only touches software that is already installed, never closes apps you have open, checks every app's version against the vendor's own feed before acting, verifies vendor downloads, and reports a result only after the live Mac confirms it.

This file is the long-form companion to https://macos-updates.64bit.site/llms.txt. All statements come from the project's own documentation (README, CHANGELOG, docs/). Current release: {{APP_VERSION}} ({{APP_VERSION_DATE}}). The site is published in English at https://macos-updates.64bit.site and in Polish under https://macos-updates.64bit.site/pl.

## Quick facts

- Name: macOS Updates (repository: macOS_updates). Current release: {{APP_VERSION}}, released {{APP_VERSION_DATE}}.
- Licence: MIT. Languages: Bash (3.2-compatible) and Python. Author and publisher: KasprowiczM.
- Platform: Apple Silicon (arm64) Macs only, macOS 13 (Ventura) through macOS 27. Intel Macs and macOS 12 or older are intentionally unsupported; setup fails before any mutation on them.
- Scope: 46 internet-downloaded apps handled through 11 update methods, plus macOS, the Mac App Store, Homebrew, native CLIs and npm.
- Quality gate: {{TEST_COUNT}} automated tests (shell syntax, Python compilation, static safety contracts, unit and registry-parity tests, secret scan).
- Terminal UI languages: English, Polish, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese.
- [Source code](https://github.com/KasprowiczM/macOS_updates)
- Documentation: https://macos-updates.64bit.site/docs, features: https://macos-updates.64bit.site/features, security policy: https://macos-updates.64bit.site/security, changelog: https://macos-updates.64bit.site/changelog, contributing: https://macos-updates.64bit.site/contributing

## Who it is for

Mac users and developers on Apple Silicon who keep a mix of Mac App Store apps, Homebrew packages, vendor-installed apps (browsers, editors, chat and AI tools, VPNs, Office, Docker) and command-line tools, and who want one auditable command instead of many separate updaters. It is a toolkit that runs locally in Terminal.

## Install

One-line installer (recommended):

    /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/KasprowiczM/macOS_updates/main/install.sh)"

The installer:

1. Clones the toolkit to `~/Dev_Env/macOS_updates` (override with `MAC_UPDATE_DIR`).
2. Shows a language picker (English menu, seven locales) and saves the choice to `.mac_update_prefs`.
3. Runs `setup.sh`: Xcode Command Line Tools, Homebrew, `mas` (App Store CLI), Python 3 and permissions.
4. Runs `build_inventory.sh`: creates `APPLICATIONS.md` from the apps already installed on this Mac.
5. Prints the update coverage report (what the project can and cannot update).

It never imports another user's inventory and never installs apps for you. Pre-clone checks (arm64, macOS version, git) run in English because localisation files are not available before the clone.

Then preview and run:

    cd ~/Dev_Env/macOS_updates
    bash update_all.sh --dry-run -y     # preview every step, mutate nothing
    bash update_all.sh                  # full update (add -y to skip the confirmation prompt)

Manual install:

    git clone https://github.com/KasprowiczM/macOS_updates.git ~/Dev_Env/macOS_updates
    cd ~/Dev_Env/macOS_updates
    bash setup.sh
    bash build_inventory.sh
    bash update_all.sh --dry-run -y

Requirements: Apple Silicon Mac, macOS 13 or later. Auto-installed by setup: Xcode Command Line Tools, Homebrew, `mas`, Python 3 (via Homebrew if missing), and optionally `rclone` if chosen as the cloud provider for the private overlay. Uninstall with `bash uninstall.sh` (removes the clone, keeps Homebrew and your apps).

## The seven steps (`update_all.sh`)

The steps always run in this order. The final macOS step runs last because `softwareupdate` may restart the Mac.

0. Prescan - discovers the apps installed on this Mac and updates `APPLICATIONS.md` (read-only scan; never blocks the run).
1. App Store - Track 1 runs `sudo mas upgrade` for the app IDs measured by the prescan, with a user-session retry. Track 2 is a separate AppleScript GUI automation for iPad apps on the Mac (for example UniFi, WiFiman, Picsart) that `mas outdated` cannot see; it first asks the public iTunes Lookup API and skips the GUI work when everything is current. Track 2 needs Accessibility permission for your terminal.
2. Native CLI and npm - existing native vendor CLIs are updated first through their own update commands (for example `claude update`, Codex, OpenCode, `agy`), then Node, Bun and global npm CLIs. Only CLIs that are already installed are updated; `--bootstrap-cli` deliberately installs missing ones. Redundant npm copies are removed only after a supported native installation is validated. Vendor CLI success requires a working `--version`.
3. Homebrew - formulae and casks with `--greedy`, plus cleanup and `brew doctor`. Cask downgrade protection compares Homebrew records with the real app bundle version; orphan casks (app deleted by hand) are detected, skipped and offered for cleanup.
4. Internet apps - the 46 apps registered in `config/internet_apps.txt`, each through one of 11 update methods (below), always after checking the vendor's own release feed.
5. Postupdate and history - refreshes `APPLICATIONS.md` and appends `UPDATES.md` atomically. It reports inventory field edits separately from observed package and CLI changes, so a table edit is never counted as an install.
6. macOS system update (final) - per-label `softwareupdate -i <label> -R`; restart-required labels go in one final batch. The step is skipped when an earlier step had a hard failure, and deferred with a warning when authorisation is unavailable. A major macOS upgrade is only installed when explicitly approved.

Only a hard failure (exit 1) in steps 1 to 4 defers the macOS step. Step 0 and step 5 never block it, and soft warnings (exit 10) never block it.

## Safety model

- Only installed software is updated. Supported-but-missing apps are reported, not installed. Apps you removed by hand are detected and never reinstalled.
- Open apps are never closed. The toolkit only launches apps that were not already running (to trigger their built-in updaters) and only quits what it launched itself. It asks the app to quit gracefully, repeating the request, and never force-kills it. An app that is running when its update would be swapped in is left untouched and reported as "quit the app so its updater can install".
- Vendor truth: each app's installed version is compared with the vendor's own feed (Sparkle appcasts, JSON, YAML or key-value feeds, GitHub releases, Google VersionHistory, Omaha logs, the iTunes Lookup API) before anything runs. Up-to-date apps are left alone. A stale vendor feed (older than what you have installed) is a warning, never a downgrade.
- Verified vendor downloads: DMGs must pass `hdiutil verify`; copied `.app` bundles must pass Gatekeeper (`spctl --assess`); the bundle identifier and Apple Team ID are validated; the new bundle is swapped in through a staged, rollback-safe replacement and mounted at unique per-session mountpoints. Any failure rolls back to the installed app.
- Honest reporting: a change is reported only after the live Mac confirms it. Unknown pending stays unknown, not zero. An updater that was launched but whose completion cannot be proven is reported as "triggered-unverified". A final message never claims "files updated" after a failure.
- `softwareupdate` must keep `-R`; `mas upgrade` must run with `sudo` (current macOS App Store CLI requirement); all code stays Bash 3.2-compatible (no `declare -A`, `mapfile`, `readarray`).
- sudo contract: at most one interactive `sudo` prompt per run (a background keep-alive refreshes the timestamp every 50 seconds), never without a controlling terminal, and never during `--dry-run`. Without a terminal, root-only steps are skipped with a soft warning instead of failing. `setup_touchid_sudo.sh` never edits `/etc/sudoers` and never grants passwordless sudo.
- Public vs private data: scripts, `config/`, docs and tests are public. `APPLICATIONS.md`, `UPDATES.md`, `.env`, `.mac_update_prefs` and `.dev_sync_config.json` are gitignored and stay on your Mac or in your own cloud storage. The common app-copy transaction never quits running applications.

## Coverage states

`bash scripts/report_update_coverage.sh` shows five evidence-based states for every installed app:

- verified direct - a package or version path, or a vendor CLI result, was confirmed.
- triggered-unverified - the app's own updater was launched, but completion cannot be asserted.
- externally managed - the App Store or the vendor owns the update lifecycle.
- manual - user action is intentionally required.
- unknown - the installed app has no registered method (add a handler, see below).

## The 11 internet-app update methods

`config/internet_app_methods.txt` assigns one canonical method per app (format `AppName|method|STATUS_VAR[|feed_url]`).

1. `keystone` - Google products only (Google Chrome, Gemini, Google Drive), driven through Google Keystone and checked against live Omaha updater status; Chrome also uses Google's VersionHistory feed to recognise a staged rollout (`rollout_hold`) as informational.
2. `github_dmg` - verified direct DMG install from the vendor release (Firefox Developer Edition, KeePassXC, Visual Studio Code, CodeEdit, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite).
3. `silent_launch` - launches the app so its built-in updater runs, and opportunistically verifies the result against a Sparkle or electron-updater feed when the bundle exposes one (ChatGPT / Codex, Claude, Antigravity, Antigravity IDE, OpenCode, Cursor, Proton Mail, Warp, Remote Desktop Manager). Without a feed it reports "launched (unverified)". Some of these (for example Cursor and OpenCode) install directly from the verified vendor feed when behind.
4. `msupdate` - Microsoft AutoUpdate's `msupdate` CLI for Excel, Word, Outlook, PowerPoint and OneNote; a package older than the installed one is held back as an upstream regression.
5. `mau_fallback_self_update` - Microsoft Teams: its own self-updater, plus an observed, verified `TEAMS21` Microsoft AutoUpdate fallback when Microsoft offers it.
6. `docker_cli` - Docker Desktop: when idle it is updated from the verified DMG in Docker's appcast without starting the engine; a running Docker is never touched because an update restarts every container.
7. `brew_cask` - Homebrew cask with `--greedy` (Brave Browser, Perplexity, LM Studio, Obsidian, ProtonVPN, zoom.us, MEGAsync, AppCleaner, Spotify, CapCut, Inkscape).
8. `appstore_gui` - App Store GUI Track 2 for iPad apps (UniFi, WiFiman, Picsart).
9. `manual` - notification only (IPMIView, DJI Assistant 2).
10. `sparkle_appcast` - checks a Sparkle appcast (Proton Drive).
11. `chromium_updater` - the vendor's Chromium updater, proven by its structured update history (Comet).

## Command-line flags (`bash update_all.sh --help` is authoritative)

- `-y`, `--yes` - skip the confirmation prompt.
- `--dry-run` - preview every step, mutate nothing, never ask for credentials.
- `--verify-only` - verify installed app versions against history without mutating.
- `--json-summary` - print a JSON result object on stdout after the run.
- `--bootstrap-cli` - explicitly install missing CLI tools (by default only installed CLIs are updated).
- `--non-interactive` - for launchd or cron; implies `-y`.
- `--notify` - post a macOS notification when the run finishes.
- `--treat-appstore-ax-as-warning` - treat App Store exit 2 (missing Accessibility) as a warning.
- `--skip-prescan`, `--skip-appstore`, `--skip-npm`, `--skip-brew`, `--skip-internet`, `--skip-postupdate`, `--skip-system` - skip steps 0 to 6.
- `--skip-doctor` - skip `brew doctor` inside the Homebrew step.
- `-h`, `--help` - usage; an unknown option exits 2.

Useful environment variables (every flag has an equivalent): `MAC_UPDATE_NONINTERACTIVE`, `MAC_UPDATE_NOTIFY`, `MAC_UPDATE_STALE_DAYS` (default 45), `MAC_UPDATE_MAX_LOGS` (default 30), `MAC_UPDATE_INTERNET_SETTLE_SECONDS` (default 10), `MAC_UPDATE_MAS_CHECK_TIMEOUT` (120), `MAC_UPDATE_MAS_UPGRADE_TIMEOUT` (1800), `MAC_UPDATE_QUIT_WAIT` (60), `MAC_UPDATE_QUIT_RESEND` (10), `MAC_UPDATE_LANG` / `MAC_LANG` (`en pl es it pt de fr`).

## Scheduled (background) runs

Two per-machine setups live outside the repository and must be done once on every Mac: Touch ID for sudo (`bash scripts/setup_touchid_sudo.sh`) and a weekly background run (`bash scripts/install_launchagent.sh --day 1 --hour 9`).

The LaunchAgent runs `update_all.sh -y --skip-system` with non-interactive mode and notifications on. It runs Homebrew, native CLI plus npm, internet apps and inventory/history. It deliberately does not run macOS system updates (Apple Silicon `softwareupdate` needs volume-owner credentials that an unattended launchd job cannot supply, and the step may restart the Mac) and does not run App Store updates (`sudo mas upgrade` needs a password and Track 2 drives the App Store GUI). Skipped steps are reported as a soft warning (exit 10), never as a failure. Run `bash update_all.sh` yourself when you want App Store and macOS updates applied.

## Exit codes

- `update_all.sh` exits 0 for a clean run or a merely degraded one (warnings such as an unverified self-updating app are the normal healthy outcome), and 1 when one or more steps failed. Use the `degraded` field of `--json-summary` to detect warnings.
- Leaf `update_*.sh` scripts: 0 clean (or dry-run), 10 soft or degraded (non-blocking), 1 hard failure (blocking).
- `update_appstore.sh`: 2 means Accessibility permission is missing for Track 2.

## Other commands

- `bash build_inventory.sh` - rebuild `APPLICATIONS.md` from this Mac (read-only scan, atomic write).
- `bash scripts/report_update_coverage.sh` - coverage report.
- `bash scripts/check_vendor_feeds.sh` - read-only inspection of vendor feeds and updater state.
- `bash scripts/scaffold_internet_app.sh "App Name" silent_launch` - scaffold support for a new internet app, then run `bash run_tests.sh`.
- `bash run_tests.sh` - the full test suite.

## Optional private overlay (`dev_sync`)

`dev_sync` syncs private files (`APPLICATIONS.md`, `UPDATES.md`, `.env`, preferences, cloud configuration) to your own cloud storage without putting them in Git. Import expands directory manifests to leaves, skips Git-tracked and excluded files, refuses symlink escapes, validates relative paths, stages accepted files, and leaves a recovery path if a swap fails. It is optional and meant for owners who keep several Macs in sync; the public installer never uses it.

## Troubleshooting highlights

- Intel Mac or macOS 12 and older: not supported.
- Wrong app list: run `bash build_inventory.sh`; never copy another user's `APPLICATIONS.md`.
- An app is not auto-updating: run `bash scripts/report_update_coverage.sh`, then add a handler.
- `mas upgrade` fails: use `sudo mas upgrade`; make sure you are signed in to the App Store.
- iPad apps "not allowed": grant Accessibility to your terminal in System Settings, Privacy and Security.
- "Quit the app so its updater can install": the update was staged but the app was open, so it was left untouched on purpose. Quit it and re-run.
- A vendor feed is stale: the vendor feed serves a version older than the installed one; the installed version is kept and a warning is shown. Inspect with `scripts/check_vendor_feeds.sh`.
- Chrome "staged rollout": informational; the update applies once Google offers it to this Mac.
- macOS step was skipped: an earlier step failed; fix it and re-run. Never replace the restart with a plain reboot; use `softwareupdate -i <label> -R`.
- Homebrew warns about the Xcode license after an Xcode update: accept it (`sudo xcodebuild -license accept`); the toolkit checks this before Homebrew runs.
- macOS 27 removes Rosetta on upgrade, so Intel-only apps stop working until Rosetta is reinstalled (and Rosetta is removed completely in macOS 28); migrate such apps to Apple Silicon builds.

## Version history (summary)

- v1.5.5 (2026-10-12, updated 2026-10-30): a Homebrew upgrade that removes `python3` mid-run no longer breaks the inventory and report step (stale command hash fixed); a failed reporting step no longer postpones macOS updates; final messages are honest (no "files updated" claim after a failure); stale-feed and quit-timeout warnings are not reported as unverified updates; toolkit-launched apps are asked to quit repeatedly, never force-killed; managed Node.js selects newest stable release; declined restart exits 10 with system_skipped_by_user; App Store Track 2 retries and soft-warns for unoffered iPad apps; Proton Drive gradual-rollout channel verified; host-tool isolation guards in test suite; 621 tests pass.
- v1.5.4 (2026-10-05): stale manufacturer feeds are separate warnings without a downgrade target or a claim that an updater launched; warning labels localised in seven languages.
- v1.5.3 (2026-10-05): ChatGPT uses its verified vendor download before GUI launch; native CLI updates run before Node and npm; running applications are protected at the bundle swap; system updates without authorisation are deferred with a warning.
- v1.5.2 (2026-09-28): Chromium updater proof from structured update history (Gemini, Google Drive, Comet); idle Docker Desktop updated from its verified DMG; OpenCode installs from the verified vendor feed; false Microsoft Teams quarantine message removed.
- v1.5.1 (2026-09-25): Chrome staged-rollout status; documentation synchronised with v1.5.0.
- v1.5.0 (2026-09-24): vendor truth release - version comparison against vendor feeds, verified direct vendor downloads with atomic swap and rollback, App Store iTunes Lookup gate for iPad apps, orphan Homebrew cask detection, only-installed native CLI toolchains, drift-free inventory synchronisation, per-label macOS system installation.
- v1.4.6 (2026-09-16): macOS 27 adaptation - Xcode licence gate, honest macOS step state and major-upgrade policy, architecture awareness and Rosetta deprecation warning.
- v1.4.5 (2026-09-07): integrity release - overlay import no longer overwrites Git-tracked files, failed swaps keep recovery data, vendor CLI success requires a working binary, unknown pending measurements are no longer shown as zero.
- v1.4.4 (2026-09-03): fixed the Claude Code native installer blocking the pipeline.
- v1.4.3 (2026-09-02) and v1.4.2 (2026-08-26): run-log review releases fixing defects that reproduced on every run and blocked real updates.
- v1.4.1 (2026-08-19): post-migration hardening after the first full run on a new Mac.
- v1.4.0 (2026-08-14): shared version utilities, Python inventory and run-summary modules, configurable inventory exclusions.

Full history: https://macos-updates.64bit.site/changelog and https://github.com/KasprowiczM/macOS_updates/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

## FAQ

Q: Is macOS Updates free and open source?
A: Yes. The public code is MIT licensed and runs locally. Machine-specific files are intentionally gitignored.

Q: Will it install apps I do not already have?
A: No. The updater only updates software already installed on the Mac. Supported missing apps are reported, not installed.

Q: Why is Apple Silicon required?
A: The project is scoped to arm64 Macs and Homebrew at /opt/homebrew. Intel Macs are intentionally unsupported.

Q: Can I preview before updating?
A: Yes. Run `bash update_all.sh --dry-run -y` or `bash scripts/report_update_coverage.sh` to inspect coverage first. A dry-run does not prove that an external GUI updater would complete.

Q: What does dev_sync do?
A: dev_sync handles optional private overlay files such as APPLICATIONS.md, UPDATES.md, .env, preferences, and cloud sync configuration. Import expands directory manifests, skips Git-tracked and excluded files, refuses symlink escapes, and leaves a recovery path if a swap fails.

Q: Why does mas upgrade use sudo?
A: The project follows the current macOS/App Store CLI requirement documented in the repo, including the CVE-related Sequoia behavior.

Q: How many apps are supported?
A: The current registry covers 46 internet-downloaded apps plus macOS, App Store, Homebrew, and CLI/npm tooling.

Q: How do I add a new internet app?
A: Use `scripts/scaffold_internet_app.sh`, register the method and dispatch order, add i18n strings, then run `bash run_tests.sh`.

Q: How do I know an update actually landed?
A: A mutation is reported only after the live Mac confirms it. Postupdate splits inventory field edits from observed package and CLI changes. Unknown pending stays unknown, not zero. A vendor CLI counts as updated only when a working `--version` exists.

Q: Does it close my open apps?
A: No. Apps you have open are never closed. The toolkit only quits apps that it launched itself, asks gracefully, and never force-kills them.

Q: Does it run on Intel Macs or older macOS?
A: No. Apple Silicon and macOS 13 or later only.
